cards.title: Ecommerce page speed: conversion, ranking and ad-spend impact
cards.summary: Why load time directly moves ecommerce revenue, Google rankings and paid-traffic ROI.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to prioritise speed work on the store roadmap, or building the business case for image, plugin and caching fixes.
steps: Frame speed as a revenue lever, not an IT chore: the source reports that even a one-second delay can reduce conversion rates by up to 7%, and that stores loading under one second can convert up to three times better than stores taking around five seconds. Treat these as source-cited benchmarks, not guarantees for your store.

Connect speed to acquisition economics: with paid ads you pay per click, so a slow landing or product page burns budget on visitors who leave before seeing the offer — speed improvements raise the effective ROI of the same spend.
Account for Google rankings: Core Web Vitals are official ranking factors, so a slow store can rank below competitors with weaker products or content.
Prioritise mobile: the source states 66% of online revenue comes from smartphones and tablets, so measure and fix mobile experience first rather than desktop.
Translate the case into a testable internal target (e.g. cut LCP or TTFB on the top-revenue templates) and re-measure conversion and bounce before/after.
caveats: The 7% conversion drop and 3x conversion uplift are reported benchmark figures from the source, not measured outcomes for any specific store; your own traffic, device mix and baseline matter.
Speed alone will not rescue bad merchandising, pricing or traffic quality — treat it as one input to conversion.

cards.title: The four Core Web Vitals to track on store templates
cards.summary: What LCP, CLS, INP and TTFB each measure, their targets, and why each matters on ecommerce pages.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing which experience metric is hurting a homepage, category page, PDP or checkout, and setting fix priorities.
steps: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) — time until the largest visible element loads, typically the homepage hero or the PDP product image. Target under 2.5 seconds. If it fails, shoppers may doubt the store's credibility or functionality before they even see the product.

CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — visual stability of elements. Target under 0.1. High CLS causes misclicks when buttons or elements move just before a tap; the source notes the worst case is purchase abandonment from frustration with an unstable interface.

INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — responsiveness to interactions such as clicking 'Add to cart'. INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024. Target under 200 milliseconds. Delayed response in checkout makes users click repeatedly or abandon because they are unsure their input registered.
TTFB (Time to First Byte) — server response time from request to first byte. Target under 800 milliseconds, which the source notes is often harder to achieve in ecommerce because of dynamic carts.
Read TTFB as a foundation signal: poor TTFB points to slow hosting or an overloaded database, and frontend work can only do so much if the base is weak.
caveats: Targets are Google's published thresholds; the source notes TTFB under 800ms is often difficult for dynamic ecommerce carts.
CLS notes about customers feeling manipulated are background context; use the misclick/abandonment mechanism when justifying fixes.

cards.title: Where ecommerce stores lose speed: five common killers
cards.summary: The recurring causes of slow storefronts — images, third-party scripts, plugins, missing caching, and unused CSS/JS.
cards.use_when: Running a speed audit on a live store to decide which fix class will recover the most seconds.
steps: Unoptimized images: high-resolution product photos are needed for sales, but PNG/JPEG inflate page weight. Modern formats (WebP/AVIF) cut file size 30–50% at the same quality. Images can make up more than 60% of a page's total data volume, making them the biggest lever.

Third-party scripts: tracking pixels, chat widgets, review platforms and social embeds each load their own JavaScript and block rendering. In many stores these external requests account for more than 50% of total load time.
Plugins: every app or plugin loads its own stylesheets and scripts. Especially harmful are plugins that run complex database queries on every page load without caching results.

Missing caching: without it, the server rebuilds each page on every click — querying databases, calculating prices, assembling layouts. Full-page caching instead serves a pre-rendered version, sharply cutting response times.
Site-wide CSS/JS: many themes load functionality on every page even when only one subpage needs it, so mobile browsers download and process unused code.
caveats: The >50% script share and >60% image data share are source-reported typical figures, not fixed proportions in every store; confirm with your own audit.
Do not remove review, chat or tracking scripts purely on speed grounds without checking their revenue or operational role.

cards.title: Baseline first: measuring speed before you change anything
cards.summary: Establish a documented before-state with PageSpeed Insights on mobile and desktop so each optimisation can be attributed.
cards.use_when: Starting any speed project on a store, or when you need evidence that a technical change actually helped.
steps: Run Google PageSpeed Insights for your URL on both mobile and desktop before touching anything, since mobile and desktop scores diverge and your mobile traffic is the larger revenue share.
Record the LCP value (and other CWV values) plus the overall score for each template you care about — homepage, key category pages, best-selling PDPs, cart and checkout.
Keep a dated change log in plain text, e.g. 'March 15 – image compression enabled', so you can tie observed metric shifts to specific actions instead of arguing about causes.
Repeat the same measurements after each change class (images, plugins, caching) rather than bundling everything, so you can tell which lever produced which gain and roll back anything that regresses.
Use the before/after numbers as the internal evidence for continuing or stopping further investment in speed work.
caveats: PageSpeed Insights is Google's tool and its interface and scoring can change — verify current reports when you run it.
Lab scores do not equal real-user field data; treat them as directional for prioritisation.

cards.title: Optimise product images with WebP/AVIF and responsive sizes
cards.summary: Convert legacy JPEG/PNG to modern formats and serve device-appropriate sizes to cut page weight 30–50%.
cards.use_when: Reducing PDP and category page weight while keeping product photography high-resolution enough to sell.
steps: Convert legacy PNG and JPEG assets to WebP or AVIF, which the source reports reduce file size by 30–50% at the same visual quality — the highest-leverage single fix when images are the bulk of page data.
For a small number of images, convert them manually with free browser-based tools; for a catalogue-scale store, use platform automation instead of hand-editing.
On Shopware 6, rely on automatic WebP generation for uploaded source images and automatic thumbnail sets that produce multiple sizes per product, so each device gets an appropriately sized file.
Keep the original high-resolution source so you can regenerate renditions if your format or size strategy changes.
Re-measure LCP on your hero image (homepage) and main product image (PDP) after conversion, since these are the elements LCP scores.
caveats: Shopware automation details are platform-specific; other carts need equivalent plugins or CDN image services — verify your platform's current capabilities.
Format support and compression results vary by image type; check visual quality on product close-ups before bulk converting.

cards.title: Plugin and script audit: earn each extension its place
cards.summary: Review your plugin list against revenue contribution, then disable, measure and delete.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up accumulated plugins, apps and marketing pixels that slow rendering on store pages.
steps: Open your plugin list in the admin panel and review it from top to bottom, asking of each one: 'How does this plugin currently contribute to revenue?'
Flag the usual offenders: marketing pixels, unused design effects, chat widgets and plugins that run uncached database queries on every page load.
Disable uncertain plugins in a staging environment — not on live — then measure page speed again and compare against your baseline.
Remove unused plugins completely rather than merely deactivating them, since leftover code and assets can still be loaded or interfere.
Repeat the loop for third-party scripts: every tracking pixel, review widget, chat tool and social embed adds blocking JavaScript, so only keep those whose measured value justifies their cost.
caveats: Never disable tracking or review scripts on live without confirming you are not breaking attribution, customer service or social proof.
Staging environments may not replicate production traffic or caching, so confirm gains on live after a controlled rollout.

cards.title: Server-side foundation: caching, PHP and HTTP/3
cards.summary: The back-end levers — Redis or Varnish full-page caching, PHP 8.2+ and HTTP/3 — that must precede frontend polish.
cards.use_when: Escalating to your host or IT team after content-level fixes, when TTFB or overall response time is still poor.
steps: Finish content and plugin work first: the source explicitly advises contacting your provider only after steps 1–3, otherwise support will simply point at your unoptimized images and scripts.

Ask specifically whether server-side caching such as Redis or Varnish is active, and whether full-page caching delivers pre-rendered HTML instead of rebuilding pages (querying databases and recalculating prices) on every click.
Ask for the current PHP version and whether your stack is on PHP 8.2+ and HTTP/3; these are the modern server technologies the source recommends as the foundation for all further optimisation.
In SaaS or cloud environments, many settings may already be optimised — still review the documentation and confirm rather than assume.
After infrastructure changes, re-run your baseline measurements for TTFB and LCP to verify the server improvement reached the storefront.
caveats: These stack recommendations reflect the source's guidance and will age; verify current supported PHP and HTTP versions before requesting changes.
Infrastructure changes can interact badly with checkout and cart logic — test transactional flows after any caching or protocol change.

cards.title: Platform-native caching and intelligent cache invalidation
cards.summary: Using built-in full-page cache, automatic WebP, thumbnail sets and selective invalidation instead of manual workarounds.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring an ecommerce platform's performance features, especially where price and stock updates must not serve stale pages.
steps: Use the platform's integrated HTTP cache so repeat visits are served pre-rendered HTML rather than re-executing PHP and querying the database.
Rely on native WebP generation for uploaded images and automatic thumbnail sets so each device receives an appropriately sized file without a custom pipeline.

Understand intelligent cache invalidation: the platform detects price or stock changes and clears only the affected pages rather than purging the entire site cache — keeping the store fast without displaying outdated prices or availability.
Confirm your platform also bundles and optimises required CSS and JavaScript, avoiding site-wide loading of code needed on only one subpage.
Where your platform lacks these features, look for equivalent automatic image conversion, responsive thumbnail generation and selective cache purging before building custom tooling.
caveats: Shopware 6 is the source's example of a platform with these native features; other platforms differ, so verify current capabilities in your own admin and documentation.
Selective invalidation depends on correct price/stock event wiring — test that price and availability changes actually propagate before trusting the cache.

cards.title: Prioritised speed roadmap for a store
cards.summary: A sequenced order of work — baseline, images, extensions, then infrastructure — so each fix can be measured and credited.
cards.use_when: Planning a multi-week speed programme and deciding what to do first with limited developer or agency time.
steps: Step 1 — Baseline: run PageSpeed Insights for mobile and desktop, log LCP and the overall score, and start a dated change log.
Step 2 — Images: convert to WebP/AVIF and serve responsive sizes, since images are typically the largest share of page data and the cheapest early win.
Step 3 — Extensions: review plugins top to bottom against revenue contribution, disable candidates in staging, measure, then delete unused ones completely and trim non-essential third-party scripts.
Step 4 — Infrastructure: with content and scripts cleaned up, ask your host or IT about PHP version and Redis/Varnish server-side caching, and confirm PHP 8.2+ / HTTP/3.
Throughout: use full-page caching with intelligent invalidation so price and stock changes clear only the affected pages, and re-measure after each stage so gains are attributable.
caveats: The sequence is the source's recommended order, not a universal law — a severely underpowered server may justify infrastructure work earlier, but expect reduced credibility with support if content is still unoptimised.
Each stage should be re-measured; bundling all changes makes it impossible to know which one helped.

08-SPD / speed and performance

Goes here. Loading performance, perceived performance, Core Web Vitals (CWV) benchmarks, the financial impact of site speed on conversion rates, server-side caching strategies (Redis, Varnish), technical mechanics of shrinking file sizes (WebP, AVIF), and platform-specific caching invalidation techniques.

Not here.

Paid advertising ROI tracking and bidding strategies -> 11-ADC

Designing the user interface or UX for checkouts -> 07-LPG

Procuring or setting up standard hosting servers -> 05-SET

Fast stores (loading under one second) convert up to three times better than slow sites (loading in five seconds). Highlighting the critical need for mobile speed optimization, as 66% of online revenue comes from smartphones and tablets. core web vitals / Understanding Google's experience metrics as official ranking factors. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP): the loading speed of the main content or hero image (target: under 2.5 seconds). Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): the visual stability of elements to prevent misclicks (target: under 0.1). Interaction to Next Paint (INP): replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024 to measure responsiveness to interactions like adding to cart (target: under 200 milliseconds). Time to First Byte (TTFB): server response time (target: under 800 milliseconds). resource optimization / Converting legacy PNG and JPEG formats to WebP or AVIF to reduce file size by 30-50% at the same quality. Utilizing platform-native automated features (e.g., Shopware 6) for automatic WebP generation, responsive thumbnail sets, and intelligent cache invalidation that clears only specific pages affected by price or stock changes.

Look for. The definition of INP (Interaction to Next Paint): the metric replacing FID in March 2024 to measure the delay in processing interactive events, with a target under 200ms. The exact WebP/AVIF file size reduction: 30% to 50% smaller than traditional JPEGs and PNGs. The definition of Intelligent Cache Invalidation: a mechanism that detects price or stock changes and selectively clears only the affected pages rather than purging the entire site cache. The specific server-side caching technologies recommended: Redis and Varnish. The recommended modern server configurations: PHP 8.2+ and HTTP/3.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.

The load time (page speed) of your ecommerce store has a direct impact on conversion rates. Visitors often abandon poorly optimized stores immediately. Well-optimized stores, by contrast, see a measurable uplift in revenue.

Page speed in ecommerce: the essentials at a glance

Why page speed matters: Even a one-second delay can reduce conversion rates by up to 7%. Fast stores (under one second load time) convert up to three times better than slow sites.

Core Web Vitals: Google measures user experience using metrics such as LCP (loading speed of the main content), CLS (visual stability), and INP (responsiveness to interactions). These metrics are official ranking factors.

Improving page speed: Optimizing images (WebP format, responsive sizes) and reducing third-party scripts (tracking, plugins).

Technical foundation: High-performance caching (e.g., Redis or Varnish) and modern server technologies (PHP 8.2+, HTTP/3) form the foundation for all further optimization.

Shopware: Shopware 6 automates many processes such as WebP generation, thumbnail management, and full-page caching.

Why page speed is so critical for online stores

In ecommerce, page speed matters because it bridges technical performance and purchasing psychology. Faster load times demonstrably lead to higher conversion rates, lower bounce rates, and stronger rankings in Google search results.

Direct impact on conversion rates: There is a clear correlation between load time and revenue. Online stores that load in under one second achieve conversion rates up to three times higher than stores that take five seconds.

Google rankings and Core Web Vitals: Google has made page speed an official ranking factor under the Core Web Vitals framework. This means a slow store will rank lower in search results even if its content or products are excellent.

Higher efficiency of advertising spend (ROI): With paid advertising (e.g., Google Ads or social media ads), you pay for every click. If a user clicks an ad but the page loads too slowly, they often leave before seeing your offer.

Mobile shopping: 66% of online revenue comes from smartphones and tablets. Page speed optimization is therefore especially critical for these devices.

Which metrics define page speed in ecommerce?

Google evaluates the speed of your store using the Core Web Vitals, a set of metrics that reflect real user experience. These include Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Time to First Byte (TTFB).

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) – perceived loading speed

LCP measures the time it takes for the largest visible element on the page (typically the hero image on the homepage or the product image on a product detail page) to fully load.

Target value: Under 2.5 seconds.

Ecommerce relevance: If the product image does not appear immediately, customers may question the credibility or functionality of the store.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) – visual stability

Buttons and other elements that shift just before a click or tap – causing users to miss their intended target – are a major source of frustration. The lower the CLS value, the more stable elements remain in place.

Target value: Under 0.1.

Ecommerce relevance: A high CLS leads to misclicks. In the worst case, customers abandon the purchase because they feel manipulated or frustrated by an unstable interface.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP) – responsiveness

INP replaced the older FID (First Input Delay) metric in March 2024. It measures how quickly the store responds to interactions, such as clicking “Add to cart.”

Target value: Under 200 milliseconds.

Ecommerce relevance: Delayed responses feel sluggish. In checkout flows, this often causes users to click multiple times or abandon the process altogether because they are unsure whether their input was registered.

Time to First Byte (TTFB) – server response

TTFB measures the time between the browser request and the first byte received from the server.

Target value: Under 800 milliseconds (often harder to achieve in ecommerce due to dynamic carts).

Ecommerce relevance: Poor TTFB indicates slow hosting or an overloaded database. If the foundation is weak, frontend optimizations can only do so much.

The biggest page speed killers in ecommerce

As a store operator, it is essential to identify what is slowing your store down. Often, the issue is not the core shop system, but elements added later – such as oversized images, scripts, or plugins.

Unoptimized images: High-resolution product images are critical for sales, but PNG or JPEG formats unnecessarily inflate page weight. Modern formats like WebP or AVIF reduce file size by 30–50% at the same quality.

Third-party scripts: Tracking pixels, chat widgets, review platforms, and social media embeds all load their own JavaScript. Each script blocks page rendering. In many stores, these external requests account for more than 50% of total load time.

Plugins: Every additional app or plugin loads its own stylesheets and scripts. Particularly problematic are plugins that run complex database queries on every page load without caching results.

Caching: Without caching, the server must rebuild the entire page on every click – querying databases, calculating prices, and assembling layouts. Full-page caching delivers a pre-rendered version instead, dramatically reducing response times.

CSS and JavaScript: Many themes load functionality site-wide, even if it is only needed on a single subpage. Browsers still have to download and process this unused code, significantly slowing mobile performance.

How to improve your ecommerce store’s page speed

Reducing load times requires minimizing file sizes, lowering the number of server requests, and implementing an effective caching strategy. This is achieved through image compression, disabling unnecessary plugins, and using modern protocols such as HTTP/2.

Step 1: Establish a baseline

Before making technical changes, you need a before-and-after comparison to understand the impact of each measure.

Approach: Use Google PageSpeed Insights. Enter your URL and run the analysis for mobile and desktop.

Tip: Take screenshots of the results or note LCP values and the overall score. Document every change in a simple list (e.g., “March 15 – image compression enabled”).

Step 2: Optimize image assets

Images can account for more than 60% of a page’s total data volume – making them the biggest optimization lever.

Action: Use modern formats like WebP instead of classic JPEGs.

Implementation: A small number of images can be converted manually using free browser-based tools.

Tip: Systems like Shopware automatically convert images into efficient formats.

Step 3: Audit extensions (plugins and scripts)

Every active plugin loads code that slows down page rendering. Over time, stores often accumulate extensions that are no longer used.

Approach: Review your plugin list from top to bottom in the admin panel. Ask yourself: “How does this plugin currently contribute to revenue?”

Check: Disable uncertain plugins in a staging environment and measure page speed again. Marketing pixels or unused design effects often block rendering. Remove unused plugins completely rather than simply deactivating them.

Step 4: The technical foundation

Some of the most powerful optimization levers sit deep within the server infrastructure.

Approach: Speak with your technical team – either your in-house IT administrator or your hosting provider’s support.

Important: Only contact your provider after completing steps 1–3. Otherwise, support will simply point to unoptimized content.

Ask specifically about the PHP version and whether server-side caching such as Redis or Varnish is active. In SaaS and cloud environments, many settings are already optimized, but reviewing the documentation is still worthwhile.
